newsitem.title: UK: Ex-WTO chief sees stalemate on workers' rights.
newsitem.headline: Ex-WTO chief sees stalemate on workers' rights.

text.p: Next month's inaugural ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation is very unlikely to make progress on the controversial issue of labour standards, Peter Sutherland, the WTO's first director-general, said on Wednesday.
Sutherland, now European head of investment bank Goldman Sachs, told the Foreign Press Association that he did not expect fireworks at the December 8-13 meeting in Singapore.

In particular, the global community was not in the mood to consider embarking on a new chapter of global trade talks so soon after the marathon Uruguay Round, which was concluded in 1994, Sutherland said.

"I don't think anybody expects the Singapore summit to bring about earth-shattering changes. We are still in the process of digesting a 22,000-page agreement, which is the biggest agreement... that the world has ever had in trade, and I don't think that there is an appetite for another Round.
"I don't think anybody is talking about another Round. I don't think that there will be another Round -- at least for the foreseeable future," Sutherland added.
He was speaking as envoys to the WTO in Geneva struggled to agree the text of a declaration to be issued by ministers.
One of the biggest sticking points is a U.S. demand that the Singapore meeting pay more than just token attention to the question of labour standards in low-wage economies.

But Sutherland said that developing countries had always been wary of admitting a link between trade and workplace conditions, seeing it as a ploy by rich nations to introduce "disguised protectionism".

"I think it's very unlikely that there'll be substantial movement forward on issues like trade and workers' rights," said Sutherland, who held the reins at the WTO for the first few months after it replaced the old General Agreements on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) in January 1995.
"There won't be a consensus. There never was anything remotely approaching a consensus on this issue in the past, and I don't see it being likely in the future," he said.

Nevertheless, Sutherland said the Singapore meeting would be an important opportunity for ministers to reaffirm their commitment to the WTO's free-trade principles and to decide which issues should take priority for the rest of the decade.
"We're talking about an assessment of progress and hopefully some movement forward in regard to a future agenda, but nothing extremely dramatic in terms of a breakthrough," he said.
The Singapore talks should also aim to give new impetus to unresolved negotiations to liberalise global trade in financial services and telecommunications, Sutherland said.
